answers.answer:
Here's where the knee stands.

Diagnosis: patellar tendinopathy, confirmed at the September 2 physio appointment. It's the same spot below the kneecap that's been flaring since the August 8 10k, so it finally has a name.

What you're supposed to be doing:

Daily eccentric decline-board squats. One slow set, about five minutes, on a decline board or a step edge. That's the whole treatment — not a gym session, a toothbrushing. Do it even on a wrecked-leg day, and do it first, before any other leg work. Your Saturday home bodyweight day is the thing to watch: if it costs you tomorrow's squats, it's too much.

No running for three weeks from September 2, so roughly to September 23. That's when you can try running again — not when the knee is done. Tendinopathy runs weeks to months, so build as if this continues past the 23rd.

Stairs still one at a time, foot flat, heel not dropping over the edge, and the elevator where there's one.

No ollies.

And when you're at physio, book the next visit before you leave the chair. Tendons don't resolve in one visit, and you're the type to treat the first one as the whole job.

One open question: the running retry lands right in the slides crunch and Rohan's last week in Toronto, so don't test the knee because the deadline is stressing you.

Here's where your knee stands:

Diagnosis: patellar tendinopathy, confirmed at the physio on September 2. Same spot I flagged back in August, so at least it has a name now.

What you're supposed to be doing:
- Eccentric squats on a decline board, daily. One slow set, about five minutes, at the edge of a step. That's the actual treatment, not an optional add-on — so it happens even on a wrecked-leg day, and it goes first before any other leg work.
- No running for three weeks from September 2, so roughly until September 23. That's when you can try running again, not when the knee is done — tendinopathy runs weeks to months.
- Push-ups and planks are fine, since they never touch the tendon.

One caution on the bodyweight stuff you started Saturday: your legs being toast after day one is a sign the leg work is stacking on top of the squats and hitting the tendon twice. Anything leg-shaped only goes in if it doesn't cost you tomorrow's squats.

answers.answer:
Ha — satay tonight, with the sink overflowing and the dishes you were about to do while the coffee brews. So the honest version: classic satay wants a marinade, skewers, and a grill, and it usually comes with peanut sauce. You're allergic to none of that[k21], but you're also not doing skewers tonight.

Fast version that's actually yours. Chicken thighs, cut into strips, tossed with soy, a spoon of curry powder or garam masala if you've got it, garlic, a little sugar, and oil. That's a ten-minute marinade, and it's fine at ten. Then either sear them hard in a pan or, since the tray's already your move[k199], spread them on a tray with the chopped veg and roast at 425 for about 20 minutes. Same tray, same method, just a different sauce story.

The sauce, no peanuts and no blender: a few spoons of peanut butter — you don't have the allergy, and this is where it goes — plus soy, a squeeze of lime, a little sugar, warm water to thin it. Or tahini instead of peanut butter if that's what's in the cupboard, which is close enough and still good.

And build the plate the way you already do: rice on the bottom, chicken and veg on top, sauce drizzled, extra on the side[k203]. That's satay, minus the skewers.

One ask: do the sink first, even just the drainer and the pan. Cooking on top of an overflowing sink is the version where this turns into takeout. How bad is it — dishes only, or is the counter buried too?

answers.answer:
Chicken satay, built for exactly your setup — base plus protein plus sauce.

Sauce first, since it's the only real work: whisk 3 tbsp peanut butter (or tahini if that's what's open), 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp lime juice, 1 tsp honey or brown sugar, 1 minced garlic clove, and a splash of warm water until it pours instead of clumps. Add chili flakes or sriracha if you want heat. That's it — no cooking.

For the chicken: cut thighs into strips, toss with soy, a little oil, garlic, and a pinch of curry powder or cumin if you have it. Either roast on the tray at 425 for about 20 minutes, or if the tray's already full, do them in a pan on the stove in one layer, a few minutes a side.

Then assemble: rice or quinoa, chicken, sauce spooned over, and something cool and crunchy if it's around — cucumber, shredded carrot, cilantro.

If you're doing this alongside the cold brew tonight, sauce while the chicken roasts. One motion, then containers and fridge.

answers.answer:
Chicken satay, quick version.

Marinade: a big spoon of peanut butter, soy sauce, a squeeze of lime, a clove of garlic grated, a bit of brown sugar, splash of water to loosen it. Coat strips of chicken thigh, give it 20 minutes if you have it, 5 if you don't.

Cook: hot pan, a little oil, 3-4 minutes a side until there's char at the edges. Don't crowd the pan or it steams.

Sauce: same thing but thicker — peanut butter, soy, lime, garlic, a little chili, warm water, whisk until it pours.

On your file though: peanut butter is the whole point of satay, and you're allergic to peanuts. So either you've got a safe jar you already use, or skip this one. Do you want me to rework it with something else as the base?
